title: Leopard men on the road in the French Cameroons
summary: A French patrol turned them back one rainy night because leopard men were out to kill; Bigard also warns that calling an African 'Bwana' invites violence.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Then we went to the French Cameroons. And this one night we was coming back to Ghana and it was raining. You couldn't see a foot in front of you it was raining so hard. And they had a French patrol on this supposed-to-be highway -- one car couldn't turn around it. So they stopped us. They said, "Where you guys going?" We said, "Well, we're going back to the hotel." They said, "Well, if I was you, I'd turn back and go where you came from because the tiger men are out"-- No, "the leopard men are out tonight."

I said, "What do you mean, leopard men?" They said, "They got leopard men. They wear leopard skins and big claws, and they're out to kill." So I said, "Yeah?" So I told the guy, "Turn." So he said, "Well, you have to go down a little farther to -- a little way. You probably can back up and then go back." He said, "Go back where you came from till tomorrow."

So that shows you how -- But we were pretty well -- we were well received. But Africa is not like, you know, you see in the movies about all that. If you call over there to somebody and say, "Bwana," they're ready to cut your head off. You know what that means?
Master. That's what it means, master. But bwana, oh, boy. You forget that word. And they really mean it, too.
